title: Messy Lab, Miracle Cure
topic: Why Alexander Fleming's messy laboratory led to penicillin

lines: Fleming shoved a greasy petri dish into his pocket, hoping to keep it safe.
He feared a clean lab would wash away his accidental experiment.
His colleagues snorted, calling him a sloppy scientist.
They warned his mess would ruin any real discovery.
Some even suggested he quit research altogether.
He left the dishes on a dusty bench while on holiday.
When he returned, a blue‑green mold had taken over one plate.
The bacteria right around the mold vanished like magic.
Fleming stared, thinking it was just a strange contamination.
He quickly set up a new experiment to test the zone.
You see, it’s like finding a clean spot on a dirty kitchen floor – the clean area stands out instantly.
The mold was Penicillium rubens, which released a substance that kills bacteria.
That substance, penicillin, proved powerful and barely toxic to humans.
Fleming published the finding in 1929, coining the name penicillin.
He imagined it could be a safe antiseptic for wounds.
Ironically, his untidy habit kept the mold alive long enough for the world to discover antibiotics.
That mess became the miracle that saved millions.

claims.claim: Fleming left staphylococci cultures on a bench; a contaminating Penicillium killed the bacteria around it.
The contaminating fungus was identified as Penicillium rubens (originally misidentified as P. rubrum).
Fleming named the antibacterial substance penicillin and noted its high potency and low toxicity.
